English sole (Parophrys vetulus) exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in size, with females attaining a significantly greater ultimate total length than males. Field surveys along the Pacific coast have documented that females reach a maximum recorded length of 57 centimeters [Li = 57 centimeters], whereas males typically do not exceed 49 centimeters [Li = 49 centimeters]. This disparity in asymptotic size is consistent with the pattern observed in many pleuronectid flatfishes, where larger female body size is associated with increased fecundity and the capacity to produce larger batches of pelagic eggs. The length at which gonadal maturation begins, commonly referred to as the size at puberty, has been estimated at 31 centimeters [Lp = 31 centimeters] from histological examination of gonad tissue across multiple year classes. Individuals below this threshold are almost exclusively immature, with no evidence of vitellogenic oocytes or active spermatogenesis in the sampled population.

Under controlled laboratory conditions that closely mimic the thermal regime of the species' nearshore nursery grounds, the embryonic development of English sole proceeds at a temperature of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C]. At this stable thermal setting, the interval from fertilization to hatching, or age at birth, was recorded as approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days] at a temperature of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C]. This relatively extended incubation period reflects the slowed metabolic and enzymatic rates characteristic of eggs developing in cold, temperate waters. Upon eclosion from the chorion, the newly emerged yolk-sac larva has a wet weight of just 0.001 grams [Wwb = 0.001 grams], a mass derived primarily from the endogenous yolk reserves accumulated during oogenesis. These lecithotrophic larvae remain entirely dependent on their yolk supply for nourishment during the first days post-hatching, gradually undergoing yolk-sac resorption as they transition toward exogenous feeding.

The reproductive output of English sole has been characterized through detailed studies of spawning adults maintained at ambient temperatures. In a series of controlled experiments conducted at 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C], gravid females were observed to release approximately 1,370 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,370 eggs per spawning event], with individual females spawning roughly once per year [F_R_i = roughly once per year]. This annual reproductive schedule aligns with the typical life history of iteroparous flatfishes inhabiting productive continental shelf ecosystems. The total annual fecundity, integrating both batch size and spawning frequency, highlights the considerable investment in offspring production that characterizes this species. The relatively modest number of eggs per spawning event, compared to some other pleuronectids of similar body size, may be partially offset by a high rate of larval survival in the cool, food-rich upwelling zones where the pelagic larvae develop and grow.

As individuals progress through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, they undergo a substantial increase in body mass that culminates in the attainment of characteristic adult weights. For females, the ultimate wet weight recorded from large, presumably senescent individuals is 1,200 grams [Wwi = 1,200 grams], a value that reflects the extensive somatic growth and energy storage required to support the production of successive annual batches of eggs. Males, which mature at a smaller size and experience lower lifetime reproductive demands, reach a maximum adult wet weight of 760 grams [Wwi = 760 grams]. The wet weight at which gonadal recrudescence is first initiated, corresponding to the onset of puberty, has been estimated from length-weight relationships at roughly 190 grams [Wwp = roughly 190 grams]. This threshold body mass marks a critical transition in the energetic allocation of the fish, signaling the shift from exclusive investment in somatic growth to the simultaneous demands of reproduction.

The maximum lifespan of English sole in natural populations has been inferred from otolith-based age determinations conducted on specimens collected during fisheries-independent trawl surveys. These data indicate that the oldest documented individuals reach approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years], a longevity that is remarkably high for a flatfish of this moderate body size and that underscores a relatively slow-paced life history at a temperature of 5.6 °C [T = 5.6 °C]. This extended lifespan, when considered alongside the deferred attainment of first reproduction at an advanced age, positions Parophrys vetulus as a species with high generation times and low natural mortality rates among adults. Comparative analyses with other Eastern Pacific pleuronectids suggest that this longevity may be linked to the cold, stable thermal environment of its preferred benthic habitat, which minimizes metabolic wear and tear. The senescence-related mortality that ultimately caps the lifespan typically follows a period of declining reproductive output in the oldest age classes.
